1391.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1391.title: 4. Architectural assessment: complexity, cost, and layer placement
1391.content: Why nothing is adopted into bootstrap (the no-outside-concept rule) . Bootstrap (bootstrap/) is the foundational, zero-dependency substrate of the entire folio-assistant platform. It defines the core data contracts and schemas that every tool, harness, and workspace inherits. | No External Dependencies: Bootstrap cannot import or depend on heavy XML parsers (for ReqIF), RDF/triple-store engines (for OSLC), or specialized NLP libraries. | Git Hygiene and Line-Oriented Diffs: Markdown front matter (.md) and lean JSON files (.json) produce readable, clean Git diffs on PR reviews. ReqIF XML produces massive, unreadable multi-thousand-line diffs for minor attribute changes. | Speed and Portability: Validating bootstrap schemas via Zod is nearly instantaneous in Bun or Node. It introduces zero runtime overhead. | Conclusion: Any standard mapping or projection must live in higher layers (cat-harness, or a content instance above it). Injecting outside formats into bootstrap would violate the repository’s foundational architecture. | . Architectural layer placement . The diagram below illustrates the strict separation of concerns across layers: . ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 2: Projection & Integration Adapters (tools / folio-assistant) │ │ - ReqIF Exporter/Importer (.reqif XML for DOORS, Polarion, Cameo) │ │ - OSLC-RM Linked Data Provider (JSON-LD / RDF / LDP) │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ maps to/from ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 1: Harness Validation & Quality Linters (cat-harness) │ │ - EARS Pattern Validator (checks statement regex / grammar in CI) │ │ - INCOSE Requirements Linter (flags vague words, compound sentences) │ │ - ISO 25010 NFR Category Checker (validates non-functional categories)│ │ - check:requirements gate & requirement-set adjudication │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ validates ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 0: Bootstrap Substrate (bootstrap/) │ │ - Pure Markdown Front Matter + Zod Schema │ │ - Zero outside concepts, zero external dependencies │ │ - 6-part requirement structure: id, title, statement, conformance, │ │ derivedFrom, successCriteria (test, inspection, review, analysis) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .

1392.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1392.title: 5. Concrete recommendations
1392.content: . | Maintain Markdown Front Matter + Zod as Native Format: . | The current Markdown front matter format for requirement documents (and JSON for programmatic requirement nodes) is optimal. | It is human-readable, machine-checkable via strict Zod schemas, and perfectly suited for Git pull request workflows. | Do not replace the front matter format with ReqIF XML or raw OSLC RDF. | . | Implement EARS Grammar Verification in cat-harness: . | Add an EARS pattern checker into check:requirements (or as a dedicated script scripts/check-ears-patterns.ts). | Every requirement statement should be checked against the 5 EARS patterns (Ubiquitous, Event-driven, State-driven, Unwanted behavior, Optional features). | This provides immediate authoring feedback and enforces rigorous syntax without changing the underlying data schema. | . | Standardize NFR Categories on ISO/IEC 25010: . | In cat-harness validators, enforce that for statements with kind: "non-functional", the category field belongs to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality taxonomy (security, performance-efficiency, compatibility, interaction-capability, reliability, maintainability, portability, safety). | . | Build Projection Adapters in Higher Layers on Demand: . | When interoperability with enterprise requirements tools is required: . | Develop tools/reqif-adapter: converts RequirementSet and Requirement nodes into standard OMG ReqIF 1.2 XML packages and vice versa. | Develop tools/oslc-rm-adapter: exposes requirement graphs via OSLC-RM JSON-LD contexts mapped through ns.jsonld. | . | Keep these tools isolated from the core bootstrap package. | . | .

1393.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1393.title: 6. What this methodology refuses
1393.content: . | Refuses adopting ReqIF XML or OSLC RDF into bootstrap/. Bootstrap must remain free of external interchange baggage. | Refuses monolithic document SRS models (IEEE 830). Requirements in this platform are atomic, graph-addressable statements (req:<slug>#<key>). | Refuses requirements without success criteria. A requirement without an explicit verification method (test, inspection, review, analysis) and criterion is unauditable and refused by CI gates. | Refuses ad-hoc NFR categories. Non-functional categories must adhere to the established ISO/IEC 25010 quality model. | .

1394.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1394.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1394.content: ← All methodologies . requirements-standards-assessment — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. Evaluating how requirements authored or verified in the harness map to or from open industry standards, interchange formats, statement grammars, and quality models — and deciding which transformations belong in higher harness layers (cat-harness, and content instances above it) while keeping the bootstrap Requirement schema strictly self-contained and free of external dependencies. It answers how bootstrap requirements translate to ReqIF, OSLC-RM, EARS, ISO 29148, and ISO 25010, what each standard costs in serialization and semantic complexity, and where mapping adapters must live. It does NOT govern runtime execution logs (prov-o-provenance), decision table structures (dmn), software package bills of materials (spdx-3), or access policy enforcement (odrl-policies). Origin. Survey and comparative assessment of formal and open requirements standards: OMG Requirements Interchange Format (ReqIF 1.2, formal/2013-10-01); OASIS Open Services for Lifecycle Collaboration Requirements Management (OSLC-RM 2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0); Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax (EARS: Mavin et al., IEEE RE 2009); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering); IEEE Std 830-1998 (Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148); ISO/IEC 25010:2011/2023 (Systems and software engineering — Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — System and software quality models); INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 4th Edition, 2023). Evaluated against the bootstrap Requirement schema (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json, Issue #1164). 1395.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1395.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1395.content: This methodology node completes bean folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (bean folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

1396.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1396.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
1396.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of bean folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to beans, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to bean IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan bean → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed beans archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

1397.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1397.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
1397.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan bean IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and beans, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

1398.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1398.title: 3. Proposed filing process (processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn)
1398.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of bean folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/sdlc/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of processes/sdlc/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings before asking a human reviewer. | If pass, proceed to BA_ReviewFiling. | . | BA_ReviewFiling — BA / Owner reviews filed requirement, organisation, and sign-off (calledElement: Process_Adjudication, skill: adjudication, fulfilment: person): . | The Business Analyst / Owner reviews the filed requirement, its concern-group placement in docs/requirements/index.md, its traceability links, and its verification evidence, deciding approve, amend, reject, defer, or cancel (adjudication-requirement-set). | . | A_RecordFilingSignoff — Record requirement-signoff attestation and set stage (skill: adjudication): . | Append the human decision to test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json and update the RequirementSet stage (accepted on approval). | . | GW_FilingAccepted — Filing accepted?: . | approve / amend → End_RequirementFiled (“Requirement filed and indexed in docs/requirements/”). | reject / defer / cancel → End_FilingHeld (“Filing held or deferred — recorded with reason”). | . | . 3.4 Open design choices put to the owner before automation is built . Before any new CLI subcommand or schema extension is built on top of check:requirements, the following three design choices from this proposal are put to the owner: . | Concern-group tagging — index-only vs schema field: . | Option A (current zero-schema-change baseline): Keep bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json unchanged (additionalProperties: false) and organise requirements by concern group in docs/requirements/index.md. | Option B (optional schema field): Add an optional "concernGroup" (or "concerns": string[] referencing code-lists/concern-group.json) to bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json so docs/requirements/index.md can be generated deterministically from front matter. | . | Enforcing in-force dependency health in check:requirements: . | Today check:requirements verifies that every dependsOn and derivedFrom target exists. Should check:requirements also fail (or warn) when an in-force requirement dependsOn a requirement whose status is retired or superseded? | . | Standalone requirement sign-off vs RequirementSet sign-off: . | Today test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json attaches to a RequirementSet (*.set.json), and a standalone docs/requirements/<slug>.md promoted via git mv only needs proposedIn. Should every filed requirement belong to a concern-group RequirementSet (docs/requirements/<group>.set.json), or remain standalone unless grouped by a CRD? | . | .

1400.title: DMN — the computable case
1400.content: Present in this repository since before this adoption, and never written down as a methodology. Five .dmn tables exist under processes/decisions/, the BPMN engine evaluates them, and dmn-authoring sits on the business-analyst role. What was missing is the statement of when a decision should be a table at all — which is what made it possible to reach for DMN by habit, or to miss it.

1401.title: The test, in one line
1401.content: Would the same inputs have to produce the same branch next month? . Yes → a table. No → a judgement, and a table would lie about its own repeatability.

1402.title: What this platform already enforces
1402.content: A hand-supplied outcome is refused. A DMN-backed gateway computes its branch from the table; an agent cannot assert which way it went. That is a stronger guarantee than the methodology itself asks for, and it is the reason a table is worth the ceremony: the decision cannot be quietly overridden at the call site. See bpmn-processes for the gateway contract and dmn-authoring for authoring the table.

1403.title: Hit policy is a modelling decision, not a detail
1403.content: UNIQUE says the rules cannot overlap and the engine may check it. FIRST says they may overlap and order decides. COLLECT returns every match. Prefer UNIQUE, because it is the only policy under which an overlapping pair of rules is an error rather than a silent precedence. FIRST makes rule order load-bearing, and a reader of the table cannot see that the order was deliberate.

1404.title: Where DMN and the other methodologies meet
1404.content: . | A kepner-tregoe analysis whose criteria turn out to recur becomes a table. That promotion is the good case, and the MADR record of the original decision is what explains why the table has the columns it has. | A table can encode which methodology applies — a decision about decisions. The repo already does this shape in folio-intent.dmn. | GRADE is not a DMN table. Certainty of evidence is a judgement over a body of evidence; tabling it would assert a repeatability the method explicitly denies. | .

1405.title: Refusals
1405.content: . | Never table a one-off to make it look rigorous. A table asserts the decision recurs; if it does not, the assertion is false and the next author will trust it. | Never hand-supply a gateway outcome. Already enforced; stated here so the reason travels with the methodology. | A table with one rule is not a decision model. It is a constant, and should be written as one. | .

1406.title: DMN — Decision Model and Notation
1406.content: ← All methodologies . dmn — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. The criteria RECUR and the inputs are data. A gateway that must branch the same way on the same facts every time. Not for a one-off judgement — that is kepner-tregoe, recorded per madr. Origin. Object Management Group, Decision Model and Notation (DMN) Version 1.5, OMG document formal/24-01-01, January 2024 (omg.org/spec/DMN). RECORDED, not held: its licence forbids posting copies on a network, so the library entry identifies the exact PDF (sha256) and its outline and holds no text. Ingested sources: . | library/omg-2024-dmn-1-5 | . Node file: dmn.md .

1407.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1407.title: Verifiable AI Guideline Evaluation: Multi-Measurement Debiased Inference, Peer Councils, and Hybrid Bounds
1407.content: Adopted 2026-10-08 (bean folio-assistant-tn3d, issue #2513). Expanded with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) public health benchmark evidence and recommendation discrepancy analysis. All eight foundational sources were ingested into library/ and verified before this methodology was adopted.

1408.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1408.title: 1. The Load-Bearing Idea, in One Sentence
1408.content: Clinical AI cannot be verified by uncalibrated model self-grading or exhaustive expert inspection: rigorous evaluation without gold standards requires decomposing multi-model error covariances, conditioning on document complexity, anchoring against known benchmark fragments, verifying decision logic on-manifold, and gating recommendation discrepancies through structured DAK decision models before executable code generation.

1409.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1409.title: 2. The Methodological Quadriad
1409.content:
Traditional evaluation paradigms fail in healthcare guidelines: . | Naive Gold Standards do not exist for newly authored guidelines (e.g. HIV PrEP L2/L3), while historical guidelines (e.g. Immunization) contain real-world conflicting statements across publication years. | Uncalibrated LLM-as-a-Judge suffers from cardinal rating drift (one rater’s “8” is another’s “6”), peer collusion, and shared prompt/inductive biases. | The Recognition vs Generation Illusion: UKHSA’s PubHealthBench (arXiv:2505.06046v4) demonstrates that while frontier models achieve >90% on Multiple Choice Question Answering (MCQA), their generative accuracy collapses to 57–74% in free-form clinical guidance advice. Direct generative authoring from narrative L1 prose into executable L3 logic is therefore inherently hazardous. | Exhaustive Human SME Review is economically impossible: WHO clinical panels cannot manually verify thousands of generated CQL lines, FHIR StructureDefinitions, and decision logic rows. | . This methodology combines four rigorous statistical and empirical pillars into an integrated evaluation engine: . flowchart TD subgraph "Pillar I: Information Limits & Noise Disentanglement" CRB["CRB Upper Bounds
(Liu & Jha 2024)
Sample-size threshold P"] CN["Correlated Noise RWT
(Liu et al. 2022)
Off-diagonal covariance C"] HYB["Hybrid Likelihood
(Liu & Jha 2026)
Anchoring Q known cases"] end subgraph "Pillar II: Debiased Multi-Model Latent Inference" DMM["DMM Framework
(Egami & Shin 2026)
CP Tensor Decomposition"] COND["Conditioning Features D_i
Text embeddings + Disagreement"] end subgraph "Pillar III: Peer Councils & Logic Verification" SVD["SVD Rating Matrix
(Nordfors 2026)
Generator V vs Evaluator U"] ANCHOR["Swept Calibration Anchors
Pinned score = 7/10"] AXE["AXE On-Manifold Fidelity
(Rawal et al. 2025)
Surrogate k-NN Emulation"] end subgraph "Pillar IV: Empirical Discrepancy & Extraction Benchmarking" REC["Guidance Recommendation Extraction
(UKHSA / Harris 2025)
Normative vs Descriptive Classification"] DISC["Discrepancy Taxonomy & FreeForm Cliff
(PubHealthBench / Harris 2026)
Extraneous | Omission | Contradiction"] end CRB --> HYB CN --> DMM HYB --> DMM COND --> DMM DMM --> SVD ANCHOR --> SVD AXE --> SVD REC --> DISC DISC --> AXE DISC --> DMM . Pillar I: Information Limits & Noise Disentanglement . | The Cramér-Rao Bound for Ranking (Liu & Jha 2024, 2403.16873): Parameterizes measurement systems as $\hat{a}{p,k} = u_k a_p + v_k + \epsilon{p,k}$, where $	ext{NSR}_k = \sigma_k / u_k$. The Fisher Information Matrix $\mathcal{I}(\Gamma)$ dictates the theoretical upper bound on correctly ranking models without ground truth. If the number of guideline recommendations $P$ is below this threshold, ranking outcomes is statistically meaningless. | Accounting for Correlated Noise (Liu et al. 2022, 2203.02010): Models joint errors across pipelines sharing foundation models via covariance matrix $\mathbf{C}$ with off-diagonal elements $\sigma_{k, k’}$. Disentangles genuine precision from shared training biases, preventing hallucinated consensus from being mistaken for clinical truth. | Hybrid Ground-Truth Integration (Liu & Jha 2026, 2603.27124): Combines unlabelled guideline extractions ($P$ patient/recommendation cases) with verified historical guideline fragments ($Q$ ground-truth anchors, e.g. validated immunization schedules): \(\mathcal{L}_{	ext{total}}(\Theta, \Sigma, \Omega) = \mathcal{L}_{	ext{unlabelled}} + \mathcal{L}_{	ext{ground\_truth}}\) Anchoring scale $u_k$ and bias $v_k$ with $Q$ known cases reduces parameter variance by over 70%, enabling high-precision ranking on small corpora. | . Pillar II: Debiased Inference without Gold Standards (DMM) . (Egami & Shin 2026, 2608.18294) When evaluating downstream clinical workflow adherence or automated DAK generation across $J \ge 3$ imperfect AI models: . | Latent true labels $X^*$ are identified via CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition without human labels. | Conditioning Set ($D_i$): To preserve conditional independence ($X^{(1)} \perp \dots \perp X^{(J)} \mid X^*, D_i, W_i$), the evaluation explicitly conditions on guideline unit features: . | Clinical complexity metrics (syntactic tree depth, clinical concept density, drug-drug interaction count). | Dense text embeddings of the input recommendation. | Multi-model disagreement scores (measuring task ambiguity). | . | Yields $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal downstream parameters $ eta$, allowing rigorous hypothesis testing (e.g. testing if Route B with KG significantly outperforms Route A without KG). | . Pillar III: Peer Councils & On-Manifold Logic Verification . | SVD Council of Peers & Swept Anchors (Nordfors 2026, 2606.21008): . | Multi-model evaluation matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{E 	imes G}$ is decomposed via SVD ($M = U \Sigma V^T$). Right singular vectors $V$ measure pure generator authoring capability; left singular vectors $U$ measure rater evaluation competence. | Swept Calibration Anchors: Every evaluation call includes an anonymized, constant reference artifact pinned at score 7/10. This anchors evaluator scale drift and restores discriminative dynamic range at the ceiling. | . | AXE: On-Manifold Logic Fidelity & Anti-Fairwashing (Rawal et al. 2025, 2505.10399): . | Evaluates extracted DAK decision tables and CQL expressions by testing whether the identified input variables allow an on-manifold surrogate (e.g. local $k$-NN) to emulate the actual recommendation output. | Adheres to three core principles: Local Contextualization, Model Relativism, and On-Manifold Evaluation. | Detects “fairwashing” and rationale hallucinations: catches when an LLM claims a clinical action was governed by valid guideline criteria when it was actually driven by irrelevant context tokens. | . | . Pillar IV: Empirical Discrepancy & Extraction Benchmarking . (Harris et al. 2025 2405.14766, Harris et al. 2026 2505.06046) . | Guidance Recommendation Classification: . | Demonstrates that extracting actionable clinical guidance requires discrete classification of narrative text chunks into normative recommendations (specific, actionable instructions/requests conditioned on patient state) versus descriptive clinical background. | . | The MCQA vs Free-Form Generative Cliff: . | SOTA LLMs achieve >90% on MCQA extraction benchmarks but drop below 75% on free-form generation, with clinical guidance demonstrating the steepest drop (o1=71%, GPT-4.1=65%, GPT-4o=60%, Claude Sonnet 3.7=57%). | Unconstrained generative pipelines introduce critical errors even when models possess underlying factual knowledge. | . | Tripartite Taxonomy of Recommendation Discrepancies: . | Type 1: Extraneous Advice: Adding clinical actions, supplementary tests, or unapproved prophylactic measures not grounded in source guidance. | Type 2: Omission of Critical Criteria: Omitting vital eligibility criteria, laboratory monitoring gates, or contraindications (e.g., immunosuppression, pregnancy). | Type 3: Contradiction & Timing Deviations: Recommending clinical interventions too early (premature treatment before diagnosis) or too late (waiting periods contradicting urgent notification mandates), or making statements directly conflicting with official policy. | . | Temporal Update Asynchrony: . | Evaluates performance degradation when guidelines undergo periodic updates (e.g. 31% of UKHSA guidance updated in 2024 post-training cutoff). Static models persistently emit superseded clinical advice unless bound to declared knowledge graph nodes. | . | .

1410.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1410.title: 3. Discrepancy Analysis in L1, L2, L3 Authoring, Editing, and Adaptation
1410.content: The WHO SMART Guidelines framework establishes a three-layer translation hierarchy: . | L1: Narrative clinical guidelines (WHO recommendations, national health ministry guidance). | L2: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) — human-readable, machine-processable operational artifacts (Personas, Workflows/BPMN, Data Dictionary, Decision Tables/DMN, Indicators). | L3: Computable FHIR / CQL Implementation Guides (Profiles, ValueSets, PlanDefinitions, Library logic). | . +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | L1: Narrative Clinical Guidelines (WHO & National MOH Guidance) | - Unstructured text, multi-guideline publications, historical revisions | - Challenge: Chunk extraction, identifying normative recommendations, cross-guideline conflicts | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | [UKHSA Recommendation Extractor + AXE Discrepancy Gating] v +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | L2: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) — The Insulating Bridge | - DMN Decision Tables: Condition-Action matrices with explicit boundaries | - BPMN Workflows: Deterministic activity sequences eliminating intervention timing errors | - Core Data Dictionary: Standardized concepts, LOINC/SNOMED codes, FHIR logical models | - Adaptation Register: Separates intentional national adaptation from accidental hallucination | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | [Deterministic Compiler Gates: cql-translation & sushi] v +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | L3: Executable FHIR Implementation Guide & CQL Library | - StructureDefinitions, PlanDefinitions, deterministic CQL evaluation engine | - Fully shielded from LLM free-form generative hallucination cliff (MCQA vs FreeForm Gap) | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ . Where Recommendation Discrepancies Arise and Fit . | Layer | Nature of Discrepancy | Mechanism for Detection & Resolution | . | L1 Authoring & Intake | Narrative Ambiguity & Cross-Source Contradiction: Divergence between WHO global guidelines and national guidance (e.g. UKHSA), or between historical editions (e.g. Measles 9mo endemic vs 6mo outbreak). | UKHSA Recommendation Classifier filters text chunks for actionable recommendations. AXE on-manifold testing identifies mutual exclusion between source assertions. Contradictions are parked in the Conflict Register (folio-clinical-conflict/v1) rather than papered over by LLM consensus. | . | L2 DAK Authoring | Logic Omissions & Intervention Timing Errors: The primary free-form failure modes identified in PubHealthBench (o1 suggesting interventions too early or too late, or omitting contraindications). | DMN Decision Tables force all conditions to be explicit; missing branches or uncovered input combinations are caught structurally. BPMN Workflows strictly fix temporal execution gates, eliminating timing drift. | . | L2 National Adaptation | Intentional Contextual Adaptation vs Hallucinated Drift: National guideline adaptations adjust thresholds based on local disease burden, drug availability, and diagnostics. | The framework cross-references adaptations against the DAK Adaptation Register. Intentional adjustments citing local epidemiological features ($D_i$) are accepted; ungrounded deviations are flagged as Type 1 or Type 3 discrepancies. | . | L3 Executable Authoring | Code Synthesis Deviations: Direct L1 $\to$ L3 translation fails due to the 25–43% generative error cliff. | L3 FHIR PlanDefinition and CQL logic are generated mechanically from L2 DMN decision tables and Data Dictionaries, completely bypassing generative free-form prompts for clinical logic. | .

1411.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1411.title: 4. Integration with Core BPMN Workflows
1411.content: The evaluation framework maps directly onto the executable BPMN workflows declared in core workflow processes: . sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Lib as Library Ingestion (ingest-derive-content.bpmn) participant Ret as Evidence Retrieval (evidence-retrieval.bpmn) participant DAK as DAK Authoring (l2-dak-authoring.bpmn) participant Rev as Change Review (content-change-review.bpmn) participant HCI as Clinical SME (editing-hci-validation.bpmn) Lib->>Ret: Extract candidate recommendation chunks (UKHSA classifier) Ret->>DAK: Multi-guideline context (Dense + TF-IDF hybrid retrieval) DAK->>Rev: Draft DMN decision tables, BPMN flows, and data dictionaries Note over Rev: Automated Discrepancy Gate: Check for Extraneous, Omission, Timing Contradiction alt Discrepancy Detected Rev->>HCI: Route to Conflict Register (folio-clinical-conflict/v1) HCI-->>DAK: SME adjudication: Intentional Adaptation vs Correction else Clean Verification Rev-->>DAK: Approve for L3 compilation (SUSHI / CQL compiler) end . Specific Workflow Gating Points . | Ingest and derive content process (ingest-derive-content.bpmn): . | Executes UKHSA-style Guidance Recommendation Classification (2405.14766) on ingested L1 sections. | Tags text chunks carrying actionable clinical recommendations with folio-guidance-recommendation/v1. | . | Evidence retrieval process (evidence-retrieval.bpmn): . | Executes hybrid retrieval combining dense text embeddings (text-embedding-3-large) and sparse lexical scoring (TF-IDF), reproducing the PubHealthBench multi-chunk context retrieval architecture to provide complete reference grounding for clinical questions. | . | Document and DAK authoring processes (authoring-a-document.bpmn & l2-dak-authoring.bpmn): . | Translates extracted L1 recommendations into DAK decision tables (dmn-authoring) and workflows (bpmn-authoring). | Ensures clinical conditions are isolated in decision tables prior to executable coding. | . | Content change review process (content-change-review.bpmn): . | Acts as Layer 2 (Agentic Council & Discrepancy Gate): . | Runs AXE on-manifold verification on proposed DMN logic. | Performs multi-model consistency checking across $J \ge 3$ model families. | Classifies candidate diffs against the tripartite discrepancy taxonomy (Extraneous, Omission, Contradiction). | . | . | Editing and HCI validation process (editing-hci-validation.bpmn): . | Acts as Layer 3 (Human SME Triage): . | Displays curated packets containing only genuine clinical conflicts, ungrounded discrepancies, and declared national adaptation choices. | Eliminates SME fatigue by ensuring all mechanical syntax and agentic consensus checks are cleared beforehand. | . | . | .

1412.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1412.title: 5. Resolution of Research Questions R1 to R7
1412.content: R1: Immunization L1 -> L2/L3 Reproduction & Conflict Register . | Evaluation Protocol: Use human-authored L2/L3 artifacts in reference SMART guideline implementations (such as immunization packages) as known ground-truth anchors $Q$. Apply Hybrid RWT (2603.27124) to estimate extraction precision $\sigma_k$ and scale $u_k$. | Conflict Register Discipline: When source guideline documents contradict each other (e.g. vaccination age thresholds in endemic vs outbreak settings): . | The pipeline does NOT invent a synthetic harmonization. | AXE (2505.10399) tests both candidate decision table branches on-manifold. If they emulate divergent recommendations from the same clinical input, a conflict is detected. | The conflict is logged directly to the Conflict Register (folio-clinical-conflict/v1) with: verbatim sources, conflict typology, proposed DAK handling rule, and audit trail, parked for Layer 3 SME adjudication. | . | . R2: HIV PrEP Clinical Complexity Axis (Unlabelled Generation) . | Evaluation Protocol: HIV PrEP represents new content with high clinical branching and no human L2/L3 ground truth. | Apply DMM (2608.18294) with $J \ge 3$ distinct model families. Condition on dense clinical text embeddings and sentence complexity metrics ($D_i$) to guarantee valid asymptotic inference without ground truth. | Verify via CRB bounds (2403.16873) that the number of extracted rules $P$ meets the ranking stability threshold. | Measure both L1 graph capture (via l1-coverage.ts) and downstream DAK products separately (DEC-007). | . R3: Knowledge Graph Value Add (Route B vs Route A) . | Evaluation Protocol: Compare Route B (Skills + Knowledge Graph) vs Route A (Skills alone, no KG) across identical model endpoints. | Model joint errors using Correlated Noise RWT (2203.02010) to eliminate foundation model correlation. | Compute the reduction in Noise-to-Signal Ratio ($\text{NSR}_B$ vs $\text{NSR}_A$). | Sub-question R3.1: Decompose value across DAK components: Core Data Dictionary (binding correctness), Decision Tables (completeness), and BPMN processes (deadlock avoidance). | . R4: Baseline Characterization (Route 0 vs Routes A & B) . | Evaluation Protocol: Benchmark Route 0 (raw unguided LLM) to establish the error baseline. | Quantify failure modes: schema hallucination, non-existent FHIR attributes, uncompilable CQL expressions, and AXE-detected fairwashing. | Incorporate PubHealthBench findings demonstrating that unguided zero-shot free-form generation exhibits up to a 43% failure rate on complex clinical guidance. | . R5: Layered Validation Feasibility & Phrasing Coverage . | Evaluation Protocol: Track filtering efficacy across the three validation layers. | Measure SME review time per packet (target: $>80\%$ reduction in SME hours). | Compute agentic agreement with final human verdicts ($\kappa$ and DMM misclassification rates). | Test phrasing coverage by evaluating variations of clinical prompt phrasing against standardized DAK personas. | . R6: Proprietary vs Open-Source KG Pipelines . | Evaluation Protocol: Feed identical L1 corpora into proprietary vs open-source KG extraction pipelines. | Benchmark node precision, relation recall, and graph completeness using RWT with correlated error correction. | Evaluate whether the marginal performance delta of proprietary pipelines justifies the vendor dependency and infrastructure cost. | . R7: Frontier vs Open-Weight Models & Benchmark Integrity . | Evaluation Protocol: Run cross-model evaluation across frontier APIs (Claude 3.7, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro) and open-weight models (Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek V3, Qwen 2.5). | Apply SVD factorisation and swept calibration anchors (2606.21008) to eliminate evaluator grading drift. | Test whether open-weight models under Route B (with KG constraint enforcement) achieve parity with unassisted frontier models under Route A. | .

1414.doc: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1414.title: Verifiable AI guideline evaluation — multi-measurement debiased inference, peer councils, and hybrid no-gold-standard bounds for clinical guidelines
1414.content: ← All methodologies . verifiable-ai-guideline-evaluation — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. Evaluating language models, knowledge-graph pipelines, and multi-agent systems on clinical guidelines (such as WHO SMART Guidelines L1 -> L2/L3 authoring, editing, and national adaptation processes, and L5 clinical workflow adherence) where gold-standard ground truth is absent, scarce, or historically conflicting, and human SME capacity is a critical bottleneck. Use it to: (1) benchmark model adherence to clinical workflows without relying on naive LLM-as-a-judge; (2) detect and classify discrepancies in clinical recommendations (extraneous advice, omissions of contraindications, timing deviations, and cross-guideline contradictions); (3) measure the fidelity and reproducibility of automated L2 (DAK) and L3 (FHIR/CQL) authoring; (4) insulate authoring from the MCQA vs free-form generative performance cliff; (5) separate intentional national/local guideline adaptation from unintentional hallucination; (6) isolate the marginal causal contribution of Knowledge Graphs (Route B vs Route A); (7) structure layered validation (mechanical -> agentic -> human SME) to protect clinical expert time; (8) operationalize automated discrepancy gating across core BPMN workflows. Not for simple single-assertion syntax checks (use mechanical compiler gates like cql-translation or sushi), and not for general software unit tests. Origin. Synthesized from eight peer-reviewed and open-access mathematical foundations for objective evaluation in the absence of gold standards and public health guideline verification: (1) David Nordfors, “The Metanym Game: An LLM Benchmark Without Ground Truth That Rises With the Models It Measures” (arXiv:2606.21008v4, 2026) — SVD of peer ratings, separating generation from evaluation skill, and swept calibration anchors; (2) Naoki Egami & Sooahn Shin, “Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements” (arXiv:2608.18294v2, 2026, MIT) — DMM framework via CP tensor decomposition conditioned on unit-level text features; (3) Yan Liu & Abhinav K. Jha, “How accurately can quantitative imaging methods be ranked without ground truth: An upper bound on no-gold-standard evaluation” (arXiv:2403.16873v1, 2024, SPIE/WashU) — Cramér-Rao bound on ranking error; (4) Yan Liu & Abhinav K. Jha, “Extending Regression Without Truth to Integrate Ground-Truth Measurements for Evaluating Quantitative Imaging Methods with Patient Data” (arXiv:2603.27124v1, 2026, WashU) — semi-supervised joint likelihood; (5) Ziping Liu, Zekun Li, Joyce C. Mhlanga, Barry A. Siegel & Abhinav K. Jha, “No-gold-standard evaluation of quantitative imaging methods in the presence of correlated noise” (arXiv:2203.02010v1, 2022, SPIE/WashU) — off-diagonal error covariance modeling; (6) Kaivalya Rawal, Zihao Fu, Eoin Delaney & Chris Russell, “Evaluating Model Explanations without Ground Truth” (arXiv:2505.10399v1, FAccT 2025, Oxford) — AXE on-manifold fidelity and anti-fairwashing principles; (7) Joshua Harris et al., UK Health Security Agency, “Evaluating Large Language Models for Public Health Classification and Extraction Tasks” (arXiv:2405.14766v2, 2025) — benchmarked recommendation extraction and clinical classification across 11 LLMs; (8) Joshua Harris et al., UK Health Security Agency, “HEALTHY LLMS? BENCHMARKING LLM KNOWLEDGE OF UK GOVERNMENT PUBLIC HEALTH INFORMATION” (arXiv:2505.06046v4, 2026) — PubHealthBench: 8,000+ questions across 687 government guidance documents, quantifying the MCQA-to-freeform degradation cliff and taxonomy of recommendation discrepancies. 1415.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1415.title: Specification-compiled agents
1415.content: Adopted 2026-09-23, on the owner’s “ingest into library for use as evidence and skills as subgraph on processes in cat-harness”. The authors’ own sentence for the mechanism: . “we compile an industry standard BPMN 2.0 process model into a ReAct style control graph. Each BPMN node provides a typed tool contract and a node local policy, while the control plane enforces branches and joins, scopes context per node, and applies contract derived runtime validation with targeted retries.” .

1416.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1416.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
1416.content: The control flow is COMPILED from a specification the model did not write, so the model never rediscovers the plan at runtime. Everything else in the paper follows from that. The model still reasons — it is a ReAct agent, not a state machine — but it reasons locally, inside a node, against a typed contract, with the branches and joins enforced by something that is not it.

1417.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1417.title: Three principles, and they are separable
1417.content: The paper names them together; they are three distinct commitments and a reader may take one without the others. | principle | what it does | what it costs | . | constrained execution | branches and joins come from the diagram, not from a plan the model produced | the diagram must exist and be right | . | targeted context management | each node sees the minimum it needs, rather than the accumulated transcript | somebody must decide, per node, what that minimum is | . | modular decomposition | prompt, tools and orchestration are generated as separate artefacts | more upfront authoring than a single prompt | . The second is the one with an argument behind it rather than an intuition. The paper cites evidence that model performance degrades as more of the context window is consumed, and observes that a generalist system cannot scope context per subtask because it does not know, at construction time, what each subtask will need. A specification does know — which is why scoping is available to this design and not to the other.

1418.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1418.title: What the paper measured
1418.content: Ten workflows, 9 to 52 nodes, all deterministic, spanning e-commerce, costing, risk, labelling, news, social, promotion, tournament registration and weather. Ten successful agents per workflow per system, evaluated across all control-flow paths — 300 agents over 30,543 test cases, from 371 generation attempts. Baselines: Roo and Cline. AutoGen, MetaGPT and FLOW were tried and produced nothing executable — MetaGPT emitted prompts and tools but no agent, AutoGen needed manual wiring even with GraphFlow, FLOW produced decompositions rather than code — so they were excluded rather than scored, which is the honest handling. Aggregates (Figure 4), specialist vs Cline vs Roo: . |   | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | tool-use exactness ↑ | 57.7 % | 48.6 % | 38.1 % | . | tool-call errors ↓ | 1.27 | 3.19 | 3.22 | . | latency (s / effective step) ↓ | 2.49 | 6.59 | 9.08 | . | process adherence ↑ | 54.7 % | 51.6 % | 42.4 % | . | repair iterations ↓ | 0.00 | 1.85 | 2.04 | . | total tokens | 53.8 k | 1 021.8 k | 1 468.6 k | . The two robust results are the last two rows, and they are robust because they are not close: zero repair iterations across every successful generation, and an order of magnitude in tokens. Those are properties of the pipeline rather than of the generated agent, which is why they do not vary the way the run metrics do.

1419.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1419.title: What the figures say that the prose does not
1419.content: Read off Figure 3 directly, 2026-09-23, as part of ingesting the images. This is a reading of the paper’s own chart, not a claim about the authors’ work, and it is recorded because the surrounding text does not say it. The paper writes of tool-use exactness that “the per-workflow breakdown in Figure 3(a) confirms this advantage holds consistently across all ten workflows regardless of complexity.” Figure 3(a) does not show that. On three of the ten the specialist system is not best: . | workflow | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | Cost | 49.6 | 76.0 | 67.6 | . | Tournament | 46.2 | 99.4 | 94.9 | . | Weather | 81.8 | 90.1 | 61.0 | . Tournament is not a near miss — it is 46.2 against 99.4. The same two workflows invert in panels (b) and (d): on Cost the specialist has the most tool-call errors (1.43 against 0.55 and 0.34) and the lowest process adherence (57.2 against 87.1 and 76.2), and Tournament repeats both. And the aggregate advantage is carried disproportionately by two workflows. On Risk the specialist shows 0.20 tool-call errors against 13.19 and 11.94, and 98.6 % exactness against 0.4 % and 0.9 %; Social contributes a smaller version of the same. A mean over ten workflows, two of which contain an order-of- magnitude gap, is a mean dominated by those two. Separately, §4.3.1 gives the aggregate repair figures as “2.08 for Roo and 1.89 for Cline” where Figure 2(d) is labelled 2.04 and 1.85. Small, and noted only because this node quotes one of them. None of this makes the method wrong. It makes the aggregate run metrics the wrong thing to quote, and it is the reason the section above marks the generation metrics as the robust pair. It also suggests a real question the paper does not ask: what do Cost and Tournament have in common that inverts the result? Looking at their diagrams, both are shallow and branch-heavy — the regime where a compiled control graph has least to contribute, because there is barely a plan to rediscover.

1420.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1420.title: What this checkout already does, and where it differs
1420.content: methodology-adoption §”Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools” requires this comparison before any tool is proposed. Read from the repository, not assumed: . | the method asks for | this checkout has | gap | . | BPMN 2.0 as the authored control flow | processes/, 69 diagrams, .bpmn as the source of truth | none — this is already the premise | . | a control plane that enforces branches and joins | workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_gate / workflow_complete, with workflow_complete refusing a step that is not enabled | none of substance | . | a node-local policy | cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement, relaxable, cat-harness.processes:decision, cat-harness.processes:judgement — four mechanisms, already finer than the paper’s one | this checkout is AHEAD | . | a typed tool contract per node | <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> names the instruction body; there is no typed input/output contract | the real gap | . | context scoped per node | not modelled. A step returns a skill; nothing says what the agent may or must see | the second real gap | . | contract-derived runtime validation with targeted retries | nothing. A step that goes wrong is not caught by the control plane | follows from the first gap | . | compilation to an executable agent | nothing, and deliberately: the diagrams here govern agents rather than generating them | out of scope, not a gap | . The last row is the one to be careful about. The paper’s system emits a deployable service; this repository’s engine runs alongside an agent doing the work. Those are different products of the same specification, and adopting the method here means taking the first three principles, not the code generator.

1421.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1421.title: Where this rendering stops
1421.content: . | No implementation is adopted. ReAct, FastAPI, LangGraph and Langfuse are the paper’s tools, not obligations. | The benchmark is not adopted. Ten workflows the authors built themselves, and they say so: “author-constructed workflows may introduce design bias”. A benchmark of somebody else’s processes measures their processes. | The numbers are not adopted as evidence for anything here. See the figures section: three of ten workflows invert, and the aggregate is dominated by two. What survives is the shape — zero repair iterations and an order of magnitude in tokens — and even those were measured on that corpus. | The deterministic scope is inherited, not argued away. Every workflow evaluated is deterministic by construction. The authors state the limit plainly; this node does not extend the result past it, and deterministic-and-agentic is where the open question lives. | “Specialist beats generalist” is not a conclusion this node draws. The paper compares one specialist pipeline against two general coding assistants operating unconstrained at their defaults, and says future work will examine “more heavily optimised baseline configurations”. That is a fair comparison of realistic low-configuration usage and it is not a claim about ceilings. | .

1422.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1422.title: The owner’s own statement of the two ends
1422.content: library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 is the owner’s deck of 2026-09-30. It is cited as evidence of intent, not of effect. Slide 7 draws the axis this node sits on: “BPMN Execution Skill: given a Process, Context, State, Role utilize one or more Skills in order [to] execute a Task”, run by either of two Tools. One is an open-source BPMN engine with “state and swimlanes strictly enforced”. The other is “an agentic swarm with ungoverned state”, mitigated by mechanical and agentic QA/QC reports. This node is the method for the first end. The deck measures nothing, so it says where the owner wants the harness to go and nothing about how well either end works. That is what the paper above is for. The diagrams this method executes are OMG BPMN 2.0.2 (formal/2013-12-09), recorded as library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2. The entry identifies the exact specification and its clause outline, so a citation can name a clause and page. It holds none of the text, because OMG’s licence forbids posting copies on a network.
